source_text:
Fragmentum in epistulam ad Philemonem (in catenis)
Phm
1,1 Ἐν πολλαῖς ἐπιστολαῖς ξένον τίθησι ῥῆμα τοῦ μέλλοντος εἰσάγεσθαι λόγου
κατασκευαστικόν, καὶ νῦν ἐπειδὴ ἔμελλεν ἀξιοῦν ὑπὲρ Ὀνησίμου τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίᾳ–
ἀξία δὲ αὐτοῦ τὸ δεδέσθαι–, τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῆς παρακλήσεως δείκνυσιν.
thought_title: Paul's strange word prepares the argument
orientation: Oecumenius is explaining why Paul mentions his imprisonment at the start of the letter to Philemon.
pass_a_gloss: In many letters he places an unusual word that prepares for the argument about to be introduced, and now since he was about to make an appeal on behalf of Onesimus by his own worth—and his worth is his imprisonment—he shows the credibility of the appeal.

choices.why: Literal rendering of ξένον as 'strange' preserves the sense of an unusual or unexpected word that Paul inserts.
The adjective modifies ῥῆμα and indicates the word's function of preparing or laying groundwork for the coming argument.
The verb here means to ask or petition, not to deem worthy; the glossary context confirms Paul is about to appeal for Onesimus.
The dative expresses the means or ground by which Paul makes the request; 'worth' follows the glossary for ἀξία.
The perfect infinitive of δέω refers to Paul's state of being in chains; glossary requires 'imprisonment' rather than a literal 'being bound.'
Both terms follow the glossary: ἀξιόπιστον as 'credibility' and παρακλήσεως as 'appeal.'

bible_refs.note: The fragment comments on Philemon 1:1, where Paul mentions his imprisonment; the source text does not quote the verse directly.

pass_b_english: In many letters Paul places an unusual word that prepares for the argument he is about to introduce. Here too, since he was about to make an appeal on behalf of Onesimus, he shows the credibility of the appeal by his own worth—and his worth is his imprisonment.

last_rejected.why: Glossary requires 'worth', 'imprisonment', 'appeal', 'credibility' only; 'strange' not banned but 'word' for ῥῆμα ignores glossary system.
last_rejected.fix: In many letters Paul places an unusual word that prepares for the argument he is about to introduce.
last_rejected.ruling: ῥῆμα naturally means 'word'; 'strange' for ξένον is standard. No meaning change or glossary break.

problems.why: Same Greek concept rendered two ways; reader may think different technical terms.
Same act described as both 'appeal' and 'request' without distinction.
problems.fix: Use one term consistently, or note equivalence.

problems.why: Three variants for same concept; 'the imprisonment' is abstract where 'chains' is concrete.
Same Greek concept rendered 'unusual' in intro but 'strange' in all commentary sections.

Changed 'the imprisonment' to 'his imprisonment' to standardize the concept.
